Coppery titi monkeys (Plecturocebus cupreus) exhibit a suite of life-history traits characteristic of small-bodied Neotropical primates with slow-paced reproductive strategies. Neonates emerge weighing just 74 grams [Wwb = 74 grams], a modest birth mass that reflects the substantial energetic investment required during the extended gestation period typical of the genus. Females experience a gestation time of 132 days [tg = 132 days]; this duration, which is intermediate among the pitheciid primates, is closely tied to the species' thermoregulatory regime, as all developmental rates reported here are referenced to a stable core body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. The relative altriciality of newborns places a premium on intensive maternal care throughout the early nursing phase. Observations from long-term field studies indicate that the suckling juvenile stage involves frequent nursing bouts, particularly during the first weeks of life, when the newborn is entirely dependent on milk for its nutritional demands. The 74 gram [Wwb = 74 gram] mass at delivery is consistent with litter sizes of one, which is the norm for this species.

Annual reproductive output in this primate is constrained by the lengthy period of dependency of a single offspring. Females produce one infant per litter [N_R_i = one infant per litter] and are capable of only a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], a low fecundity that is compensated by high parental investment and extended offspring care. The relatively low reproductive rate is further underscored by the fact that infants are not nutritionally independent until reaching weaning at 206 days after birth [tx = 206 days after birth], all measured against the species' standard body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. The dietary transition from milk to solid foods occurs gradually, with infants beginning to accept small fruits and insects around three months of age, though maternal provisioning continues regularly until the weaning milestone is attained. This prolonged nursing period aligns with the comparatively slow life-history profile of the coppery titi, a pattern observed across other members of the Callicebinae subfamily.

Adult body size in Plecturocebus cupreus is modest compared to many other platyrrhine primates, yet their mass is substantial relative to other pair-living monogamous species. This adult mass is achieved gradually, as juveniles undergo a prolonged growth phase that delays the onset of sexual maturation. Sexual maturity is attained at 1096 days after birth [tp = 1096 days after birth] for females, whereas males reach puberty somewhat earlier, at 638 days after birth [tp = 638 days after birth]; both milestones are recorded at the species' characteristic thermoneutral temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. The dimorphism in maturation timing is noteworthy, with females deferring reproductive competence by an additional 1.25 years relative to males, a pattern that may reflect the greater energetic demands of gestation and lactation.

Longevity records from both wild and captive settings indicate that the coppery titi possesses a relatively extended lifespan for a primate of its size. The maximum lifespan recorded in captivity approaches 9,636 days [am = 9,636 days] when maintained at a core temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This remarkable longevity, exceeding predictions based on body mass alone, is thought to be linked to the species' low extrinsic mortality rate in its dense forest habitat, as well as its monogamous social system, which buffers individuals against certain predation risks. The onset of physiological senescence is typically gradual, with reproductively active adults continuing to breed well into their second decade of life. Field-caught individuals show minimal wear on dentition even at advanced ages, suggesting that the species experiences low rates of dietary abrasion. This extended life history is consistent with the slow pace of life that characterizes the entire genus, where high adult survival offsets the consistently low annual fecundity.

Comparative analyses of pitheciid reproductive biology have highlighted the coppery titi as an informative species for understanding the evolutionary trade-offs between gestation length and neonatal development. These interconnected life-history metrics underscore a tightly coevolved strategy in which slow growth, extended parental investment, and exceptional longevity are mutually reinforcing.
